Default.title: Volunteer astronomers spot a new comet from a car park in Lowmarsh
Default.tldr: A club of amateur stargazers in the fictional town of Lowmarsh has found a comet professional surveys missed.
Default.content:
A group of amateur astronomers in the fictional town of Lowmarsh has discovered a comet that larger professional surveys appear to have missed.

The Lowmarsh Stargazers, who meet every clear Thursday in the car park behind the leisure centre, noticed a faint smudge near the constellation of Cassiopeia while testing a second-hand camera. Over the following three nights they photographed it moving against the background stars, and sent their measurements to the made-up International Comet Registry.

The registry confirmed the find on Tuesday. Under its rules the comet will carry the club's name, making it Comet Lowmarsh, the first object in the sky named after a town best known for its roundabout.

The club's chair, a retired postwoman, said the discovery was down to patience rather than equipment. "Most of us have cheap telescopes and expensive flasks," she said. "The flasks matter more. You have to be willing to stand in the cold for a long time looking at nothing."

The comet is not expected to become visible to the naked eye. It will make its closest approach to the Sun next spring, and the club has offered to lend its telescopes to anyone who wants a look.

This story is a made-up sample for trying Truman. None of it happened.

Jimmy.title: Pensioners find comet, astronomers find excuses

Jimmy.content:
A club of amateur astronomers in Lowmarsh has found a comet the professionals missed. The professionals say they were busy. Busy doing what? It's space. The one thing it's got is time.

They spotted it from a car park behind the leisure centre, which is the most Lowmarsh sentence ever written. The comet will be named Comet Lowmarsh, which is a lot of pressure for a ball of ice. It's never been to Lowmarsh. Nobody has. Not on purpose.

Ricky.title: Car park comet: amateurs embarrass the experts
Ricky.tldr: A bunch of people with flasks found a comet. Good for them, honestly.
Ricky.content:
Look, I love this. A bunch of retired people standing in a freezing car park every Thursday, and they find a comet the actual scientists missed. The scientists with the satellites. The funding. The lanyards.

The chair of the club says the secret is a good flask. That's it. That's the whole of astronomy apparently. Meanwhile the comet gets named after Lowmarsh, which it'll never visit, which makes it smarter than most of us.

This is a made-up sample story.

Default.title: Retired engineers build free prosthetic hands in a church hall
Default.tldr: A group of retired engineers in the made-up town of Calderbrook has fitted more than 300 children with 3D-printed hands.
Default.content:
In a church hall in the fictional town of Calderbrook, a group of retired engineers has spent four years building prosthetic hands for children, and giving them away.

The group, which calls itself the Tuesday Workshop, began when one member's granddaughter was born without fingers on her left hand. Commercial prosthetics cost thousands and children outgrow them within a year, so he designed one he could print at home for the price of a sandwich.

Word spread. The workshop now has eleven members, six 3D printers and a waiting list. It has fitted more than 300 children, each hand sized from photographs and finished in the colours the child chooses. The most requested design, by a distance, is one that glows in the dark.

The hands are simple: the wearer bends their wrist and the fingers close around an object. They cannot do everything a commercial prosthetic can. But the workshop says that matters less than you would think, because a hand a child can replace for free every six months is a hand they actually wear.

The group has published its designs so that others can copy them, and says it has heard from workshops in nine countries that have.

"We spent our careers making things nobody thanked us for," one member said. "Pumps. Valves. Gearboxes. This is the first thing I've made that gets a drawing in return."

This story is a made-up sample for trying Truman. None of it happened.

Jimmy.content:

The most popular design glows in the dark. Which is the best thing about it, and also the worst thing to discover at 3am.

They've put the designs online so anyone can make them. Retired engineers, being generous with their time. Usually they're being generous with their opinions about your boiler.

Three hundred of them. In a church hall. And the kids pick the colours, and loads of them want glow-in-the-dark, which is exactly what I'd have wanted.

One of them said he spent his whole career making pumps and nobody thanked him, and now he gets drawings. That got me, that did. Made-up sample story.

Default.title: Hospital waiting list falls for a third month
Default.tldr: Waiting times in the made-up Northvale health region are down 12% since the summer.
Default.content:
The waiting list for planned operations in the fictional Northvale health region has fallen for the third month in a row, down 12% since July.

The region's health board puts most of the fall down to two changes. Operating theatres now run on Saturdays, using staff who volunteered for extra shifts at a higher rate. And patients waiting for hip and knee replacements are now offered a date at whichever of the region's four hospitals can see them first, rather than the one nearest their home.

About a third of patients offered a hospital further away have taken it. The board says those who did were treated, on average, eleven weeks sooner.

Clinicians welcomed the figures but warned that winter usually reverses the trend, as beds fill with emergency admissions. The board says it has kept twenty beds aside for planned operations this year to stop that happening.

The longest waits are still in dermatology and ear, nose and throat, where the list has barely moved. The board says those specialties are short of consultants rather than theatre time, and that Saturday sessions cannot fix that.

This story is a made-up sample for trying Truman. None of it happened.

Default.title: Divers find a 200-year-old cheese in a shipwreck, and decline to taste it
Default.tldr: Archaeologists recovered a sealed wheel of cheese from the made-up merchant ship Margery.
Default.content:
Divers exploring the wreck of the fictional merchant ship Margery, which sank off the made-up Gannet Point in 1824, have recovered an intact wheel of cheese sealed in wax inside a lead-lined box.

The ship was carrying cheese, wine and wool to the continent when it struck rocks in a storm. Most of its cargo was lost or salvaged at the time, but the box was buried under a collapsed section of deck and only came to light when last winter's storms shifted the sand.

The team brought the box up in July and opened it last week in a laboratory at the fictional Gannet Maritime Museum. Inside was a wheel of hard cheese about the size of a dinner plate, its wax still unbroken.

The museum's food historian said the find could show how cheese was made and stored for long voyages, which is poorly recorded. Samples will be tested for the bacteria and moulds it contains, some of which may no longer exist in modern cheese.

Asked whether anyone would try it, the dive team's leader was firm. "No," she said. "Absolutely not. We've had a lot of questions about that, and the answer is no."

The cheese will go on display next year in a sealed, refrigerated case.
